A.explanation: At $0.5\text{ m}$ displacement is zero on a falling slope, so a small shift to the right makes the particle move up with maximum speed.

B.explanation: At $1.0\text{ m}$ the rope is at the trough with maximum negative displacement, so particle velocity is momentarily zero.

C.explanation: At $1.5\text{ m}$ displacement is zero but on a rising slope, so the particle has maximum downwards velocity for rightward travel.

D.explanation: At $2.0\text{ m}$ the rope is at the crest with maximum positive displacement, so particle velocity is momentarily zero.

hints: Notice the graph is displacement against distance in $\text{m}$ at one instant, with wavelength $2.0\text{ m}$ and zero crossings near $0.5\text{ m}$, $1.5\text{ m}$ and $2.5\text{ m}$.
For a wave travelling to the right, particle velocity is $ -v \times$ slope, so a downward slope means upward motion and speed is largest where the slope is steepest.
Compare the slopes at $0.5\text{ m}$ and $1.5\text{ m}$: both are at zero displacement but one slope gives upward motion and the other gives downward motion.
walkthrough: Read the axes: vertical is transverse displacement and horizontal is distance from $0$ to $3.0\text{ m}$. The arrow shows the wave pattern moves to the right.
Recall two rules: particle speed is maximum at equilibrium ($\text{displacement}=0$) and zero at crests and troughs, and direction follows what the approaching wave brings.
Imagine the whole cosine-like pattern shifted a little to the right. Points on a downward-sloping section are replaced by higher points from the left, so they move up.

Points on an upward-sloping section are replaced by lower points from the left, so they move down. Hence upward velocity occurs between $0$ and $1.0\text{ m}$ and between $2.0\text{ m}$ and $3.0\text{ m}$.
Maximum speed needs the steepest slope, which is at the zero crossing. Between $0$ and $1.0\text{ m}$ this is at $0.5\text{ m}$, where motion is upwards with maximum speed. This is option A.
